# Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026: permitting reform tracker

> Section index, plain-language summaries, verbatim quotes with page and line cites, and a comparison with the SPEED Act and the Energy Permitting Reform Act of 2024. Bill text released 2026-09-30; 417 pages, 71 sections. Data as of 2026-10-01.

- Site: https://pranava0x0.github.io/permittingreform/
- Bill PDF (official): https://www.epw.senate.gov/public/_cache/files/5/c/5c5f5935-b224-48e7-abea-e60c30e7a4cf/7935BF3C85967B6F56F6F4858FD3221B7E0AEB02D04BE391CAFBD1B884CE3DC5.bipartisan-american-affordability-and-jobs-act-text.pdf
- Source data: https://github.com/pranava0x0/permittingreform

## Sections

- Sec. 1101. Purposes; procedure; savings provision (pp. 4 to 5): Rewrites NEPA's opening section. Adds a statement that NEPA prescribes a procedure for considering and informing the public about the reasonably foreseeable environmental effects of major federal actions, producing an informational document, and a savings clause that NEPA mandates no particular outcome.
- Sec. 1102. Definitions (pp. 5 to 25): Moves NEPA's definitions from section 111 to a new section 3 and expands them. New terms include agency chief environmental review and permitting officers, eNEPA technologies, key permitting agencies, a 20-page record of stakeholder engagement, record of decision, and statement of purpose and need.

The bill lists 14 kinds of action that are not major federal actions and so fall outside NEPA. A project whose only federal involvement is a loan or loan guarantee is out. So are routine administrative actions under $10 million, and repair or replacement of lifeline infrastructure that adds no more than 20 percent capacity.

The list also excludes geothermal observation test projects, transmission upgrades under new Federal Power Act section 216A(b), covered Natural Gas Act pipeline work, actions another agency already evaluated, and Army Corps continuing-authority or environmental-infrastructure projects with a federal share of $50 million or less.
- Sec. 1103. Implementing procedures (pp. 25 to 26): Requires every federal agency to update its NEPA regulations, procedures and policies within 180 days of enactment, directs the CEQ Chairman to standardize agency procedures, and lets the Chairman give technical assistance.
- Sec. 1104. Cooperation of agencies; reports; availability of information; recommendations; international and national coordination of efforts (pp. 26 to 27): Conforming edits to NEPA section 102(2): agencies must develop methods consistent with data and technology standards for eNEPA technologies, and 'responsible official' becomes 'lead agency'.
- Sec. 1105. Procedure for determination of level of review (pp. 28 to 31): Expands when an agency can skip an environmental document. An agency may apply one or a combination of categorical exclusions (but may not stack the same size-based exclusion repeatedly), may rely on a categorical exclusion Congress created, and may treat a state or tribal environmental review, or compliance with another federal law, as serving NEPA's function. A project sponsor can ask the lead agency to stop an environmental assessment and go straight to an environmental impact statement. If the lead agency decides no environmental document is needed, no other agency may prepare one.
- Sec. 1106. Timely and unified Federal reviews (pp. 31 to 61): Rewrites NEPA section 107, the core of the review process. Environmental assessments are due in 1 year and environmental impact statements in 2 years, measured from the earlier of the agency's determination or its notice that the application is complete. A record of decision follows a final EIS within 45 days. Agencies in the review must decide all authorizations within 90 days, and agencies outside it within 120 days.

Lead agency designation gets a clock, with the CEQ Chairman resolving disputes within 21 days by a final, unreviewable decision. The Chairman can also order a resolution of interagency disputes, and that order counts as full compliance with any interagency consultation obligation under federal law.

The lead agency must drop any alternative that does not meet the purpose and need or the goals of a non-federal sponsor. Agencies need not consider science published after the notice of intent. Public scoping comment periods run 45 to 60 days, or 75 with the sponsor's consent.

If an agency defies a Chairman's dispute order and a deadline is missed, then after 30 days its permitting officers and senior executives must spend at least half their workweek on the overdue review. Once any deadline is 60 days overdue, the agency head may not travel more than 25 miles from the duty station until the document or permit issues. The Secretary of Defense is exempt. Project sponsors can sue over missed deadlines. The court must rule within 120 days and can order a decision within 60 days.
- Sec. 1107. Programmatic environmental document (pp. 61 to 62): Doubles the shelf life of programmatic environmental documents from 5 years to 10 years before an agency must reevaluate them.
- Sec. 1108. Use of categorical exclusions by other agencies (pp. 62 to 64): Requires every agency to report all its categorical exclusions to CEQ within 30 days and each new one within 7 days; CEQ keeps a public register on its website. An agency may adopt another agency's exclusion after consulting it and documenting the adoption.
- Sec. 1109. Applications for authorizations (pp. 64 to 67): Sets an application clock: within 60 days an agency must say whether an application is complete, and within another 60 days it must tell the sponsor whether the action is excluded from NEPA, needs an environmental assessment, or gets a notice of intent for an EIS. Applicants must submit a list of all known permits, a record of stakeholder engagement, and a statement of purpose and need.
- Sec. 1110. Judicial review (pp. 67 to 74): Adds a judicial review section to NEPA. Suits challenging an authorization on NEPA grounds must be filed within 150 days. The party must allege an actual or imminent injury amounting to direct harm. Where a comment period was offered, the party must also have filed a sufficiently detailed comment. The federal court of appeals for the circuit where the project sits gets original and exclusive jurisdiction, with random judge assignment.

If a court finds a NEPA violation, the only remedy is remand without vacatur or injunction, with a fix deadline of no more than 180 days. The permit stays in effect and the project can proceed during the remand. A preliminary injunction is available only for a likely violation of a law other than NEPA or the National Historic Preservation Act.

Courts must give substantial deference to agencies on the scope and content of environmental documents. No NEPA suit may be brought over an action on tribal trust lands unless the tribe itself sues or effects reach beyond trust lands. No suit may rest on an omission from the sponsor's stakeholder engagement record.
- Sec. 1121. Council on Environmental Quality (pp. 74 to 96): Replaces NEPA section 209 with an eNEPA technology mandate. Within 60 days CEQ must publish data standards for permitting data, within 120 days guidance on minimum functional requirements (automated project screening, case management, GIS tools, AI-assisted comment analysis, administrative-record tools), and agencies must begin implementing within 180 days. CEQ and the key permitting agencies build an ePermit unified interagency data system and a public authorization portal hosted by GSA. A pilot is due within a year and the system by December 1, 2028, 'to the maximum extent practicable'. Congress gets access to the AI prompts and fine-tuning data agencies use. CEQ also sets outcome-based performance measures for agencies and staff. Authorizes $5 million a year for NEPA.
- Sec. 1131. Definitions (pp. 96 to 97): Definitions for the permitting tracker subtitle. A 'transparency project' is any action that needs an EIS, or an environmental assessment still unfinished 13 months past its deadline.
- Sec. 1132. Environmental Review and Permitting Tracker (pp. 97 to 101): Requires CEQ, with GSA, to run a public Environmental Review and Permitting Tracker listing every EIS project within 14 days of its notice of intent, with location, purpose and need, sponsor and agency contacts, quarterly schedule-compliance status explaining every slip and who caused it, and litigation status.
- Sec. 1133. Permitting Improvement Fund (pp. 101 to 102): Creates a Permitting Improvement Fund at Treasury that CEQ can transfer to permitting agencies for detailees, training, project managers, standardized processes, and public engagement. Authorizes $20 million a year for fiscal years 2027 through 2033.
- Sec. 1201. Water quality criteria (pp. 102 to 103): Requires EPA to use notice-and-comment rulemaking when it develops Clean Water Act water quality criteria, and routes challenges to those criteria and to any definition of 'waters of the United States' directly to the federal courts of appeals.
- Sec. 1202. Clean Water Act permitting and State certification (pp. 103 to 122): Rewrites Clean Water Act section 401 state certification. Certification is limited to water quality requirements. A state may deny only on clear and convincing evidence that no condition could make the project comply, and may impose only conditions that are necessary, least burdensome, and consistent with the federal permit.

The process gets a prefiling meeting, a defined complete application, a 3-day receipt acknowledgment, a 90-day completeness notice, and a review period of up to 1 year that can be extended only if the applicant asks in writing and the certifying authority agrees in writing. Silence is a waiver. Denials must name the specific water quality requirement violated. On judicial review the burden of proof falls on the state by clear and convincing evidence.

For interstate gas pipelines and bulk-power transmission lines, certification covers only direct point source discharges and must be decided within 9 months.
- Sec. 1203. Permit term for NPDES permits (pp. 123 to 123): Extends the maximum term of state-issued NPDES discharge permits from 5 years to 10 years.
- Sec. 1204. Permits for dredged or fill material (pp. 123 to 128): Limits EPA's section 404(c) veto to the period between a complete application and permit issuance. Extends nationwide permits from 5 to 10 years, lets the Corps modify them mid-term, and requires it to keep nationwide permits 12, 14, 43, 57 and 58 for projects filling under 2 acres, which are deemed a minimal adverse effect. Reissuing a nationwide permit needs no Endangered Species Act consultation, only a programmatic environmental assessment under NEPA, and no National Historic Preservation Act consultation, so long as the permit does not loosen preconstruction requirements.
- Sec. 1205. Judicial review timeline clarity (pp. 128 to 133): Adds a 150-day statute of limitations for challenges to section 404 permits, general permits, verifications and state program approvals. Where a draft was published with at least 30 days for comment, a plaintiff must have commented on the issue. Remedies are limited to remand, with vacatur or injunction available only on a finding of imminent and substantial danger to health or the environment. Remand deadlines are capped at 180 days.
- Sec. 1301. Definitions (pp. 133 to 134): Defines 'best scientific and commercial data available' in the Endangered Species Act as all relevant, objective information at the time of the action, including models that account for error and are applied without policy presumptions.
- Sec. 1302. Timeline for Section 7 consultations (pp. 134 to 136): Shortens ESA section 7 formal consultation from 90 to 60 days, and the applicant-consent extension from 150 to 100 days. If consultation stretches past 145 days without the applicant's written consent, the applicant may sue under the APA for agency action unlawfully withheld. Consultation on any project with a NEPA document must finish by the NEPA deadline, unless the Secretary grants an extension for extraordinary circumstances.
- Sec. 1303. Projects in the operational right-of-way (pp. 136 to 137): Exempts highway and transit projects in an existing operational right-of-way that are categorically excluded from NEPA under MAP-21 section 1316 from ESA section 7 consultation and conferencing.
- Sec. 1304. State assumption of consultation responsibilities (pp. 137 to 154): Creates ESA section 7A letting the Interior Secretary assign section 7 consultation duties to a state, by written agreement, for projects entirely inside the state. Interior must propose a rule within 270 days. States must show legal, financial and staffing capacity, waive sovereign immunity, accept federal court jurisdiction, keep public-records laws comparable to FOIA, and meet the same deadlines as the Secretary. Interior audits annually for 4 years, can terminate after a 120-day cure period, and applicants may still choose federal consultation. Interior's failure to act on an application within 180 days counts as a failure to act under the NEPA sanctions section.
- Sec. 1305. Judicial review (pp. 154 to 155): Lets any person seek review of a biological opinion in the D.C. Circuit within 150 days after it is made public.
- Sec. 1306. Listing determinations (pp. 155 to 155): Requires the Secretary to accept and integrate state-collected data in listing and delisting decisions when it meets the best-available-data standard.
- Sec. 1307. Authorization of appropriations (pp. 155 to 155): Authorizes $150 million a year for fiscal years 2027 through 2031 for Endangered Species Act section 7 consultation and for state participation in the program under section 7A.
- Sec. 1308. National Fish and Wildlife Foundation Coastal State Fund (pp. 156 to 158): Creates a National Fish and Wildlife Foundation Coastal State Fund granting money to coastal states for coastal resource and natural infrastructure programs, allocated 70 percent equally, 15 percent by tidal shoreline and 15 percent by coastal population density, capped at 5 percent per state. Authorizes $50 million a year for fiscal years 2028 through 2032.
- Sec. 1401. Maintaining Federal authorizations or permits for projects with non-Federal sponsors (pp. 158 to 166): For projects with non-federal sponsors, a federal agency may not revoke, suspend, amend, or otherwise interfere with a federal authorization in effect on or after September 16, 2026.

There are five exceptions. A court can order the action. The holder can have materially breached the permit or the law, or obtained the permit by fraud. The action can be needed to prevent specific, urgent, substantial and proximate harm to life, property, national security or defense, based on new information not considered in the original review. Or the holder can ask for it.

Agencies must give written notice with the statutory authority and evidence. The sponsor can sue in district court, where the agency carries the burden by clear and convincing evidence and classified information is reviewed in camera. A winning sponsor gets the permit reinstated, an injunction against repeat interference without a court order, attorney fees, delay costs, and an additional 25 to 50 percent of all project costs incurred, paid from the Judgment Fund without appropriation.

Where a stop-work order issued within the year before enactment was enjoined, the same judge keeps jurisdiction.
- Sec. 1402. Ensuring fairness for specific types of covered projects (pp. 166 to 182): Creates a cause of action for applicants in 46 named energy project types, plus any similar type a court certifies. The list runs from onshore and offshore wind, solar and storage to coal, gas, oil, nuclear, geothermal, transmission, pipelines, mining, hydrogen, hydropower, LNG and carbon storage.

The applicant must show a 'pattern of disparate treatment': an intentional, statistically demonstrated rise in denials or delays for that project type, compared with the prior 5 years. The pattern must last 180 days after enactment for permits without a NEPA document, or 280 days for those with one. Executive orders and official statements showing bias count as supporting evidence. The government must produce 5 years of raw statistics or face an adverse inference.

Permits for these projects that need no NEPA document must be decided within 1 year of a complete application.

Remedies are an injunction, fees, economic damages, and 50 to 100 percent of the expected construction cost, paid from the Judgment Fund. The applicant must finish the project or repay. Class actions are barred, and suits cannot be filed until 180 or 280 days after enactment.
- Sec. 1403. Avoiding unreasonable delays in permitting (pp. 182 to 185): Gives applicants for permits that need no environmental document a right to sue in district court when the 1-year deadline in section 1402(c) is missed. The agency is excused if it proves the delay was caused by a disaster, a national emergency, fraud, withheld information, or a lapse in appropriations of more than 14 days. Courts decide within 120 days and can order a decision within 60 days.
- Sec. 2101. Transmission permitting (pp. 185 to 200): Overhauls FERC's backstop siting authority under Federal Power Act section 216. FERC must issue a construction or modification permit for an interstate line of 230 kilovolts or more, or an advanced-conductor line at a voltage FERC sets, when it makes the required findings. The line no longer has to sit in a national interest corridor designated by the Energy Department. The state's clock for deciding now starts on the date the application is filed with the state.

FERC must find the line is in the public interest, protects or benefits consumers, and improves reliability. For lines of 345 kilovolts or more the developer may file at FERC at the same time as at the state. FERC must take landowner input, consider the state record, and give a 45-day comment period.

Costs go only to customers who benefit, in line with cost causation, and customers with no or trivial benefit cannot be charged involuntarily. Clean Water Act section 401 certifications and other state approvals under federal law become 'Federal authorizations' coordinated by FERC as lead agency (Interior for offshore), with challenges heard in the courts of appeals. ERCOT is excluded.
- Sec. 2102. Reconductoring and other activities in existing rights-of-way (pp. 200 to 205): Adds Federal Power Act section 216A: work that maintains or increases grid capacity inside an existing right-of-way (reconductoring, higher operating voltage, added circuits, advanced transmission technologies, added storage at an existing facility, a parallel circuit) is categorically excluded from NEPA, is not a major federal action, and is not an undertaking under the National Historic Preservation Act. It also amends Natural Gas Act section 7 so that repair, replacement, looping, compression and capacity-enhancement of interstate gas pipelines inside an existing right-of-way or previously reviewed footprint are not major federal actions or historic-preservation undertakings.
- Sec. 2103. Transmission planning (pp. 205 to 218): Adds Federal Power Act sections 224 and 225. The Energy Department studies transmission constraints and congestion every 3 years and may identify constrained geographic areas. FERC must issue a rule within 180 days requiring every planning region to file a regional planning process and joint interregional processes with its neighbors within 2 years, updated every 4 years. The processes must use common assumptions, a fixed list of six benefits, and selection criteria of improved reliability, consumer benefit and public interest.

Costs are allocated to beneficiaries roughly commensurate with benefits. Compliance with the FERC planning orders published on June 11, 2024, December 6, 2024 and April 28, 2025 (Order 1920 and its two rehearing orders) counts as compliance for regional planning. A project selected in a regional or interregional plan is deemed to meet most of the findings for a FERC backstop permit. Approving a planning process is not a major federal action under NEPA.
- Sec. 2104. Improvements relating to local transmission planning and development (pp. 218 to 224): Adds Federal Power Act section 226. One or more states may refer a utility to FERC for an investigation of its local transmission planning. FERC forms an investigative team with up to 3 state appointees. If the team finds the utility's process is not selecting the more efficient or cost-effective local projects, or is crowding out regional planning, FERC may order process changes, cut the utility's return on equity on local projects, remove the presumption of prudence, or fine the utility up to $5 million per imprudent facility, payable to the referring state.
- Sec. 2105. Prohibition of right of first refusal (pp. 224 to 224): Bans any federal right of first refusal for transmission facilities selected in a regional or interregional plan for cost allocation, overriding any FERC rule or order to the contrary.
- Sec. 2106. Consolidated planning process (pp. 224 to 226): Requires FERC, within 18 months, to make each planning region file a consolidated interconnection and transmission planning process that looks 20 years ahead, publishes fuel-neutral planned interconnection locations with a fixed per-megawatt cost, and runs a cluster study with one decision point and nonrefundable security to deter speculative projects. Regions file within 2 years and update every 2 years.
- Sec. 2107. Ratepayer protection (pp. 226 to 240): Congress finds it is not just and reasonable to charge data center, AI and cryptocurrency loads less than the embedded and incremental cost of the transmission they need. FERC must revise its 1994 transmission pricing policy within 270 days, propose a rule 270 days after that, and finish within a further year.

New Federal Power Act section 228 covers data center loads of 20 megawatts or more. None of the incremental cost of serving them (generation, transmission, distribution) may be recovered from other customers. Recovery continues even if the data center leaves, and utilities must collect financial assurance before building upgrades.

States may charge these loads more than cost and credit the surplus to other ratepayers. They may run open seasons that award service by ratepayer benefit, whatever the queue order. They may require the load to bring new generation, require curtailable service, and treat data centers less favorably than other industrial customers. The section applies to loads interconnecting after enactment.
- Sec. 2108. Dispatchable energy systems market access (pp. 240 to 259): Opens wholesale markets to aggregations of customer-sited batteries, fuel cells and generators that can respond within 15 minutes (5 kilowatts minimum per device, 100 kilowatts per aggregation). After 18 months, grid operator rules that block them are unjust and unreasonable. Grid operators file compliance tariffs within 180 days. Unless state law or the state regulator provides otherwise, distribution utilities in organized markets must interconnect these resources. They must also accept wholesale metering data.

A device paid by a state retail program cannot be paid twice for the same service; FERC orders disgorgement and can impose penalties of up to 3 times the amount for each day it was knowingly kept. The Energy Department runs a voluntary streamlined local permitting program for rooftop solar, batteries and vehicle chargers, with $20 million a year authorized for fiscal years 2026 through 2031.
- Sec. 2109. Advanced transmission technologies (pp. 260 to 265): Requires FERC to make public utilities use advanced transmission technologies, including best-available conductors, dynamic line rating, power flow control and topology optimization, in new and upgraded lines, with a presumption that the cost is prudent. FERC issues a rule within 1 year requiring recurring benefit-cost evaluations; when benefits exceed costs the utility must deploy on FERC's timeline or face a penalty such as a lower return on equity.
- Sec. 2110. Expediting generator interconnection queues (pp. 265 to 266): Directs FERC to start a rulemaking within 1 year requiring transmission providers to share and use computing technologies, including AI and automation, to process interconnection requests faster, and to revisit the rule every 4 years.
- Sec. 2111. Grid data access (pp. 266 to 272): Adds Federal Power Act section 232. Transmission providers must hold the data needed for interconnection and facilities studies and may demand it from any bulk-power system user, owner or operator, who must respond in 15 days in a usable format. Confidentiality rules can shape access but cannot be used to withhold data. Violations are treated as reliability matters. FERC and the Energy Department publish, within 1 year, a reference specification for fully automated interconnection studies.
- Sec. 2112. Power marketing administrations (pp. 272 to 278): Lets the federal power marketing agencies set pay outside the federal schedule, benchmarked to consumer-owned utilities in their interconnection, to fix hiring and retention problems.
- Sec. 2113. FERC fee assessments (pp. 278 to 278): Requires FERC to review every 5 years whether its fees and charges are enough to handle its workload promptly and report to Congress.
- Sec. 2114. Collection of data on computational load entities (pp. 279 to 279): Directs the Energy Information Administration to revise Form 861 to collect electricity load from data center entities (AI, cloud, cryptocurrency) at least 90 days before the first April 1 after enactment.
- Sec. 2115. Conforming amendments; savings provision (pp. 280 to 280): Conforming cross-references in the Federal Power Act and a savings clause: nothing in the transmission title gives FERC authority over retail electricity sales or local distribution.
- Sec. 2201. Accelerating claims (pp. 280 to 286): A 150-day statute of limitations for any lawsuit challenging a federal agency's grant or denial of an authorization for an energy, carbon dioxide, mineral or wildfire fuel-reduction project, unless the underlying law sets a shorter one. Covered authorizations include leases, drilling permits, rights-of-way, mining plans, Endangered Species Act statements and permits, and forest restoration approvals. Agencies must publish the decision within 3 days. Courts must expedite the case, and a remand cannot give the agency more than 180 days unless the law requires longer. Agencies must tell the project sponsor about any suit within 30 days.
- Sec. 2211. Permitting compliance on non-Federal land (pp. 286 to 290): Removes the federal drilling permit requirement for oil and gas wells on non-federal surface land where the federal government owns less than half the minerals in the drilling unit, or where the wellbore only enters or passes through federal minerals. Lessees notify Interior of state permits. Interior cannot require bonds, mitigation or reclamation approval on that non-federal land. Royalties are unchanged; Indian lands are excluded.
- Sec. 2212. Rights-of-way across Indian land (pp. 290 to 298): Lets an Indian tribe grant rights-of-way across its own tribal land without Interior Department approval, if the grant follows a tribal regulation that Interior has approved. The tribal regulation must include an environmental review with public comment. Interior has 180 days to approve or disapprove, and its approval is not subject to NEPA, the National Historic Preservation Act or the Endangered Species Act.
- Sec. 2213. Accelerating renewable energy permitting (pp. 298 to 304): Interior or the Forest Service must tell an eligible-project applicant within 30 days whether its right-of-way application is complete. If an EIS is needed, the agency has 90 days after finding the application complete to issue a notice of intent. Within 30 days after a complete application is submitted, it must issue any required cost-recovery agreement and grant, deny or defer the application. Deferral requires notice of remaining steps and agency timelines.

Within 180 days, both departments must develop or adopt categorical exclusions for listed low-disturbance renewable activities, with extraordinary-circumstances exceptions. The list includes previously analyzed disturbances under 5 acres, certain repeat activities, small solar projects, surveys and meteorological towers. BLM must issue standard renewable review standards within 2 years.
- Sec. 2214. Electric grid projects (pp. 304 to 305): Directs Interior and Agriculture to adopt, within 180 days, categorical exclusions for placing power lines in approved corridors, for upgrades and reconductoring of existing lines in existing rights-of-way or on previously disturbed land, and for battery storage on previously disturbed land.
- Sec. 2215. Hardrock mining mill sites (pp. 306 to 318): Lets a hardrock mine operator locate as many 5-acre mill sites on public land as are reasonably necessary for waste rock, tailings and other operations under an approved plan of operations, for a $400 annual fee per site. Mill sites convey no mineral rights and cannot be patented. Hardrock minerals on acquired federal lands become leasable. Mill site fees and those lease receipts go to a new Abandoned Hardrock Mine Fund for cleanup.
- Sec. 2221. Geothermal observation test projects (pp. 318 to 325): Requires a categorical exclusion within 1 year for geothermal observation test wells on existing leases that disturb no more than 10 acres, use no permanent roads, and finish within a year. Casual-use activities need only 30 days' notice and are not major federal actions.
- Sec. 2222. Geothermal royalties (pp. 325 to 329): Calculates the reduced early-years geothermal royalty per generating facility, starting from each facility's in-service date, so a second plant on an old lease gets its own 10-year lower-royalty period.
- Sec. 2223. Geothermal leasing reform (pp. 329 to 332): Requires geothermal lease sales every year instead of every 2 years, with a replacement sale in the same year if one is cancelled, and sets 30-day completeness and 30-day decision deadlines for geothermal drilling permits.
- Sec. 2224. Geothermal ombudsman and permitting task force (pp. 332 to 338): Creates a Geothermal Ombudsman and a Geothermal Permitting Task Force inside BLM within 60 days to resolve disputes between field offices and applicants, move staff to offices with backlogs, and pay retention allowances of up to 25 percent of basic pay.
- Sec. 2225. No Federal permit required for geothermal activities on certain land (pp. 338 to 341): No federal drilling permit for geothermal exploration and production on non-federal surface where the United States owns less than 50 percent of the subsurface geothermal estate, if the operator files its state permit with Interior. Indian lands are excluded; royalties are unchanged.
- Sec. 2226. Effect of pending civil actions on processing applications relating to geothermal leasing (pp. 341 to 342): Requires Interior to keep processing geothermal permits, sundry notices and rights-of-way under a valid lease despite pending litigation, and to decide within 60 days of completing legal requirements, unless a court has vacated or enjoined the lease or permit.
- Sec. 2227. Cost recovery from geothermal leasing, permitting, and inspections (pp. 342 to 346): Lets Interior charge geothermal applicants and lessees for the cost of processing and inspections through September 30, 2033, with hardship reductions, and requires a report within 5 years.
- Sec. 2228. Publication of Gold Book for geothermal operations on Federal land (pp. 346 to 348): Directs Interior to identify standard geothermal procedures within 1 year and then publish, within 270 days, an updated and renamed 'Gold Book' of surface operating standards that covers geothermal, reviewed every 5 years.
- Sec. 2229. NEPA Review (pp. 349 to 351): Rewrites section 390 of the Energy Policy Act of 2005. The five listed oil and gas activities (small surface disturbances, drilling at an existing pad, drilling in a developed field, pipelines in approved corridors, minor maintenance) are no longer treated through categorical exclusions; they are declared not to be major federal actions at all, and geothermal is added. The corridor look-back for pipelines goes from 5 to 10 years, and geothermal gets a new item for power lines up to 20 miles in an approved corridor. Drilling permits for these activities carry no NEPA requirements.
- Sec. 2231. Identifying and removing market barriers to hydropower (pp. 351 to 354): FERC, with the Energy Department, reports to Congress within 270 days on market barriers to hydropower and pumped storage and on how to pay hydropower for the grid services it provides, after a technical conference and public comment.
- Sec. 2232. Certain conditions on issuance of licenses (pp. 354 to 354): Limits the mandatory conditions federal land agencies can attach to a hydropower license under Federal Power Act section 4(e) to those 'reasonably related to the effects of the project'.
- Sec. 2233. Hydropower maintenance and temporary adjustments (pp. 354 to 357): Bars FERC from requiring license amendments for routine hydropower maintenance, repair or replacement, or for temporary operating variances caused by events outside the licensee's control. FERC must propose a rule within 90 days and finish within a further 180 days defining which alterations are substantial enough to need approval. Dam safety authority is preserved.
- Sec. 2234. Micro hydrokinetic energy projects (pp. 358 to 362): Creates an expedited FERC license of 10 to 20 years for micro hydrokinetic projects of 5 megawatts or less (wave, tidal, current and free-flowing river turbines with no impoundment), with final action within 1 year of the application and categorical exclusions for low-disturbance activities.
- Sec. 2241. Federal Energy Regulatory Commission staffing (pp. 362 to 362): Widens FERC's special pay authority to economic and legal positions and strikes the consultation requirement in paragraph (6) of the same subsection.
- Sec. 2242. Northwest Power and Conservation Council (pp. 362 to 362): Amends the cap on Bonneville's funding of the Northwest Power and Conservation Council, section 4(c)(10)(B) of the Northwest Power Act, by adding the words 'since the date of enactment' of this bill.
- Sec. 2243. Federal Energy Regulatory Commission personnel safety (pp. 363 to 363): Lets FERC authorize its employees to perform law enforcement duties to protect the Chairman and Commissioners.
- Sec. 2251. Offshore energy (pp. 363 to 364): Amends the offshore renewable energy section of the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act. Interior's duty changes from 'prevention of interference with reasonable uses' of the ocean to 'prevention of unreasonable interference with other uses'. Interior may grant rights-of-way for electric transmission through national marine sanctuaries, with sanctuary permits lasting as long as the right-of-way. The Inflation Reduction Act's link between offshore wind leasing and oil and gas lease sales is preserved.
- Sec. 2252. Offshore energy transmission (pp. 365 to 371): Directs Interior and Energy to identify preferred routes for offshore transmission cables within 2 years and review them every 3 years, makes Interior the lead agency for offshore transmission permitting, requires a final rule within 2 years, and lets Interior issue offshore transmission rights-of-way competitively or noncompetitively.
- Sec. 2301. Historic preservation (pp. 372 to 413): Rewrites section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act. An 'adverse effect' must be reasonably foreseeable and must directly alter a historic property. Temporary alterations are excluded. Visual, atmospheric and audible effects are excluded unless they directly and significantly diminish the property. An 'undertaking' excludes projects whose only federal tie is a loan, guarantee or grant, the non-federal parts of a project, minor repairs, permit renewals and post-approval operations.

The process gets deadlines: 30 days to decide whether a project is an undertaking, 60 days for the agency's report, 90 days for a determination, then 60 days of consultation, 45 days for Advisory Council comments and 30 days for a final decision. Consultation must be finished by the time the NEPA document is completed, unless the Secretary grants an extension for extraordinary circumstances. State and tribal preservation officers who do not respond in 30 days are passed over, and the agency may decide in its sole discretion that other considerations outweigh preservation.

Courts give substantial deference and may only remand without vacatur or injunction; a preliminary injunction is available only for a likely violation of another law. Claims go to the courts of appeals, within 150 days, from parties who commented and suffered direct harm. A suit over a missed consultation deadline goes to a court where the project is located. Non-signatories cannot challenge programmatic agreements. State and tribal programs are evaluated every 2 years and lose grants if they miss consultation timelines.
- Sec. 2302. Funding for the Historic Preservation Fund; use and availability; grants for Tribal Historic Preservation officers; additional funding (pp. 414 to 417): Authorizes $200 million a year for deposit in the Historic Preservation Fund for fiscal years 2027 through 2036. Deposits become available the next fiscal year without a further appropriation. Creates a $20 million-a-year grant program (fiscal years 2027 through 2030) for tribal historic preservation officers to build online databases of records and of properties of traditional religious or cultural importance, with protections against disclosing sensitive site locations.

## Timeline

- 2023-06-03: Fiscal Responsibility Act writes NEPA deadlines and page limits into law (BUILDER Act)
- 2024-07-31: Senate ENR Committee advances the Manchin-Barrasso Energy Permitting Reform Act, 15-4
- 2024-11-12: D.C. Circuit panel says CEQ has no authority to issue binding NEPA regulations
- 2025-01-20: EO 14154 'Unleashing American Energy' directs CEQ to propose rescinding its NEPA rules
- 2025-01-20: EO 14156 declares a national energy emergency and calls for emergency permitting
- 2025-01-20: Presidential memo halts new wind leasing and orders review of wind permitting
- 2025-02-03: North Dakota court vacates CEQ's 2024 NEPA rule, finds CEQ lacks rulemaking authority
- 2025-02-25: CEQ interim final rule removes its NEPA implementing regulations from the CFR
- 2025-04-11: FERC Order No. 1920-B affirms the long-term transmission planning rule on rehearing
- 2025-04-15: Presidential memo orders permitting technology plan and CEQ Permitting Innovation Center
- 2025-04-16: Interior orders construction stopped on Empire Wind off New York
- 2025-04-23: Interior adopts emergency permitting procedures with 14- to 28-day energy reviews
- 2025-05-19: Interior lifts Empire Wind stop-work order; Burgum cites New York pipeline capacity
- 2025-05-28: CEQ withdraws Biden-era NEPA guidance on greenhouse gas emissions and climate change
- 2025-05-29: Supreme Court, 8-0 in the judgment, narrows NEPA review in Seven County v. Eagle County
- 2025-07-03: Interior, DOE, USDA, DOT and Army Corps replace NEPA rules with streamlined procedures
- 2025-07-04: One Big Beautiful Bill Act adds a paid, faster NEPA review option (Sec. 60026)
- 2025-07-15: Interior memo routes every wind and solar decision to the Secretary for final review
- 2025-07-23: EO 14318 directs faster federal permitting for data centers and their power supply
- 2025-07-25: Westerman and Golden introduce the SPEED Act (H.R. 4776) to rewrite NEPA
- 2025-08-22: BOEM orders Revolution Wind to halt all offshore activity at about 80% completion
- 2025-09-22: Judge Lamberth enjoins the Revolution Wind stop-work order
- 2025-09-29: CEQ issues updated NEPA guidance and a template for agency NEPA procedures
- 2025-10-22: Whitehouse says it makes little sense to pursue permitting reform if the administration won't faithfully execute it
- 2025-10-23: DOE directs FERC to start a large-load interconnection rulemaking for data centers
- 2025-11-20: House Natural Resources Committee advances the SPEED Act 25-18
- 2025-12-08: Federal judge vacates Trump's wind permitting freeze as arbitrary and capricious
- 2025-12-09: Heinrich, Whitehouse and Schatz publicly oppose passing the House SPEED Act
- 2025-12-11: House passes the PERMIT Act 221-205 after unanimous ePermit Act vote
- 2025-12-18: House passes the SPEED Act 221-196 after text changes demanded by offshore wind opponents
- 2025-12-22: Interior pauses leases for five offshore wind projects under construction
- 2025-12-22: Senate Democrats Whitehouse and Heinrich end permitting talks over offshore wind halt
- 2026-01-08: CEQ finalizes removal of its NEPA regulations, adopting the 2025 interim rule unchanged
- 2026-01-08: Menendez and Casar introduce Data Center Transparency Act (H.R. 6984)
- 2026-01-12: Federal judges enjoin all five offshore wind stop-work orders between Jan. 12 and Feb. 2
- 2026-01-15: EPA proposes revised Clean Water Act Section 401 certification rules
- 2026-01-15: Van Hollen introduces Power for the People Act (S. 3682)
- 2026-01-28: Senate EPW permitting hearing: Whitehouse ties progress to administration's wind policy
- 2026-02-03: House members introduce FREEDOM Act to bar presidents from revoking permits
- 2026-02-11: Hawley and Blumenthal introduce the GRID Act (S. 3852)
- 2026-02-19: Permitting Council signs first state FAST-41 agreements with Idaho and Tennessee
- 2026-03-04: Seven hyperscalers sign White House Ratepayer Protection Pledge
- 2026-03-05: Whitehouse and Heinrich reopen permitting negotiations, warning against 'further mischief'
- 2026-03-13: Administration does not appeal ruling against the Revolution Wind stop-work order
- 2026-03-23: Interior and TotalEnergies sign deal to cancel two offshore wind leases; talks continue
- 2026-03-25: Senate ENR hearing on the bulk power system takes up transmission and data centers
- 2026-04-09: CEQ issues new categorical exclusion guidance, replacing its 2010 guidance
- 2026-04-09: Tonko introduces House companion H.R. 8241
- 2026-04-21: Judge Casper enjoins five directives that stalled federal wind and solar permitting
